title: Serial execution: Redis MULTI, WATCH and Lua
goal: By the end, you can explain how running transactions one at a time on one thread makes them safe without locks, why that only works when each transaction arrives complete, which Redis tool (MULTI/EXEC, WATCH, a Lua script or a pipeline) makes a sequence of commands safe and which only makes it fast, and what splitting the data across threads costs.

warmup.q: Redis runs every command on one thread and takes no locks. Two copies of the payments program handle purchases on the same prepaid card at the same moment. Each runs `GET balance:7` to read the balance, subtracts in its own code, then runs `SET balance:7 <new value>` to write it back. Can a debit be lost?
options: No: with one thread, only one copy's code runs at a time
Yes: the thread runs each command alone, but the other copy's commands can run between one copy's GET and its SET
No: Redis holds the key for a program between its GET and its next SET
Only if Redis's extra network threads are switched on
warmup.why: One thread makes each command a transaction of its own, run from start to finish with nothing in between. A GET and a later SET are two commands, so both copies can GET 100 before either one SETs, and one debit disappears. Only what arrives as one unit runs alone, which is why engines like this want the whole transaction at once. Redis never holds a key for anyone between commands. Its optional I/O threads only read and write network messages, and the commands still run on one thread.

sections.h: One thread, one transaction at a time, and no locks
sections.body:
The last four lessons built a lot of machinery: row locks, lock queues, versions and snapshots, a deadlock detector and SSI's notes. All of it exists because transactions run at the same time. (A transaction is a group of changes that counts as one.) Here's the blunt alternative: run them one at a time. One thread, a single line of work inside a program, takes a transaction, runs it to the end, and only then takes the next. That's **serial execution**. The result always equals some one-at-a-time order, because that's what really happened. There are no locks, no deadlocks and no transactions aborted for clashing. In the café's terms, the barista is the thread, and each order is a transaction.

For decades nobody built databases this way, for two reasons. Data lived on disk, and a transaction that waited 10 ms for a disk read left the only thread idle. So a database needed many transactions running at once to keep the processor busy. And transactions were interactive: the program sends a command, thinks, then sends the next.

Two things changed. Memory got cheap enough to hold all the data in use, so a transaction no longer waits for the disk. And the everyday transactions of a business, an order or a payment, turned out to be tiny. In 2007, Michael Stonebraker's group at MIT looked at TPC-C, a standard test that runs the orders of a made-up wholesale company. Its heaviest transaction reads about 200 records, under a millisecond of work in memory.

Their prototype database, H-Store, split the data into partitions, separate parts with one thread each, and used no locking at all. On the same machine with two processor cores, it ran 70,416 TPC-C transactions a second, against 850 for a tuned commercial database. H-Store became a product, VoltDB. Redis also runs every command on one thread, as Inside an in-memory store: how Redis executes commands, in the Caching track, showed.

Where does it break? The thread must never wait. When the data is in memory, the slowest part of a transaction is the program on the other end, the client. Say the database needs 10 µs (millionths of a second) of work for a transfer. But the client drives it one step at a time: read the balance, decide in its own code, then write and commit (make the change final). That's two round trips, each a message there and an answer back, of about 0.5 ms inside one data center (a building full of computers).

If the database keeps its thread for the transfer until it commits, the thread waits 1 ms for 10 µs of work. The ceiling is about 1,000 transfers a second, however fast the processor. If instead it serves other clients between the steps, the transfer is no longer alone.

So serial engines, the databases built this way, want the whole transaction at once, as code they can run to the end without waiting. That code is a **stored procedure**. VoltDB's procedures are Java classes, and Redis's are scripts in Lua, a small programming language. That's the model for this lesson: **one thread, and each transaction arrives complete.** The Try it measures what one Redis thread does when work arrives that way. The rest of the lesson asks the practical question: what can you send at once, and what happens to the parts you can't?

try.title: Measure what one thread can do
steps: From the `labs` folder, start Redis with `docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d`. (Docker runs programs in sealed boxes called containers.) `redis-benchmark`, a load-testing tool, ships in the same image, so these commands run the client and the server in one container, talking over the loopback interface, the computer's network connection to itself.

Run the four benchmarks below. The first uses one client that waits for each reply, and the second uses 50 clients. The third uses 50 clients that each pipeline 16 commands, sending them without waiting for each reply. The fourth runs a whole transfer (read, check, debit and credit) as one Lua script per request.
Before each one, predict whether it's faster or slower than the one before, and by roughly how much.

code.title: from the labs folder
code.src:
docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli MSET acct:a 100000000 acct:b 0
docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-benchmark -q -t set -n 20000 -c 1
docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-benchmark -q -t set -n 200000 -c 50
docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-benchmark -q -t set -n 1000000 -c 50 -P 16
docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-benchmark -q -n 200000 -c 50 \
  EVAL 'local b = tonumber(redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) or "0") if b < tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end redis.call("DECRBY", KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) redis.call("INCRBY", KEYS[2], ARGV[1]) return 1' 2 acct:a acct:b 1

try.expect:
Two runs on the lab laptop (each benchmark prints progress lines, then this summary):

```text
SET: 26881.72 requests per second, p50=0.039 msec        one client, waiting for each reply
SET: 227790.42 requests per second, p50=0.103 msec       50 clients
SET: 1848428.75 requests per second, p50=0.367 msec      50 clients, pipelines of 16
EVAL ... 2 acct:a acct:b 1: 193236.72 requests per second, p50=0.215 msec
```

The second run gave 26,525, 209,864, 1,886,793 and 187,441. `p50` is the median time per request: half the requests were faster. One thread can run almost 1.9 million SETs a second, but a client that waits for each reply gets about 26,000, because the thread sits idle for most of every 39 µs round trip. The transfer script runs about 190,000 complete transactions a second on that one thread, with no locks and no retries. The numbers move with your processor and with what else Docker is running, and the ratios stay similar.

sections.h: Two commands from your program are two transactions
sections.body:
Redis treats each command as a transaction: its one thread runs it to the end, with nothing in between. A sequence of commands from your program is not one transaction. Between your commands, Redis's event loop, the loop that serves every connected client in turn, runs other clients' commands. In the terms of the first section, a sequence is an interactive transaction, and Redis chose to serve others while you think.

Here's the card from the opening. Redis stores each value under a name, its key, and the card's 100.00 sits under the key `balance:7`. Big apps run several copies of their program on different machines, so payments keep flowing if one machine fails. (Many companies call each running copy a pod, and this lesson's pictures do too.) Two purchases reach two copies at the same moment, 30.00 at a café and 50.00 at a fuel station. Each copy does what looks right: GET the balance, check it, and SET the new one.

```java
long balance = Long.parseLong(redis.get("balance:7"));
if (balance >= amount) redis.set("balance:7", String.valueOf(balance - amount));
```

```kotlin
val balance = redis.get("balance:7")!!.toLong()
if (balance >= amount) redis.set("balance:7", (balance - amount).toString())
```

Here `redis` is a connection to Redis, made by a client library (code that does the talking for your program), and `get` and `set` send one command each. The Kotlin version is the same two lines; `!!` says the balance must exist.

Both GETs can run before either SET. Both copies read 100, and one writes 70, the other 50. The SET that runs last wins. The card has paid 80.00, and the balance shows 70.00 or 50.00. That's a **lost update**: one write replaced another that it never saw. The simulator below lets you make it happen, with T1 and T2 as the two copies. Run both GETs first.

The café picture breaks here. A barista who heard "what's on my card?" and then "set it to 70" would notice the queue in between. Redis serves every order alone, and it doesn't remember who asked what.

Why not one command? For a change that needs no decision, there is one. `DECRBY balance:7 30` reads, subtracts and writes inside a single command, so it can't lose an update. But a payment must not take the balance below zero, and `DECRBY` doesn't check. From 20, `DECRBY balance:7 30` cheerfully answers -10. The decision needs a read, a test and a write, with no other client's write in between.

One command runs alone, and a sequence doesn't. Redis gives you three ways to send more at once. MULTI/EXEC sends a batch. WATCH checks a decision your code made from an earlier read. A Lua script sends the decision itself, the stored procedure of the first section. Next, we'll take them in that order.

sim.title: Two pods debit one prepaid balance
sim.intro: T1 and T2 are two pods. Each reads the balance, subtracts in its own memory, and writes the result back. 100 - 30 - 50 should leave 20. Can you end with 70?

goal.say: Lost update: the card paid 80 euros and the balance only went down by 30. Both pods read 100 before either wrote, and T1's SET overwrote T2's without ever seeing it.

try.title: Lose a debit by hand
steps: From the `labs` folder, open redis-cli, Redis's command-line program, in two terminals: `docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli` (start the server first if needed).

Play the race. Terminal 1 runs `SET balance:7 100` and `GET balance:7`, and terminal 2 runs `GET balance:7`. Terminal 1 writes the café debit, `SET balance:7 70`, and terminal 2 writes the fuel debit, `SET balance:7 50`. Then read the balance.
Now try the one-command version in either terminal: the last four commands. Predict the last answer.

code.title: two redis-cli prompts (the order to type them)
code.src:
SET balance:7 100
GET balance:7
GET balance:7
SET balance:7 70
SET balance:7 50
GET balance:7
SET balance:7 100
DECRBY balance:7 30
DECRBY balance:7 50
DECRBY balance:7 30

try.expect: Both GETs print `"100"`, both SETs print `OK`, and the final `GET balance:7` prints `"50"`: 80.00 paid, 50.00 taken off. With `DECRBY`, nothing is lost (`(integer) 70`, then `(integer) 20`), but the third debit cheerfully answers `(integer) -10`. One command can't lose an update, and it also can't refuse to overdraw.

sections.h: MULTI/EXEC sends a batch, and WATCH checks a decision made in your code
sections.body:
The plainest way to send more at once is a batch. `MULTI` tells Redis to start queuing: every command after it answers `QUEUED` instead of running. `EXEC` then runs the whole queue as one step on the event loop, so no other client's command runs in the middle. Redis calls this a transaction, and a transfer from account `acct:a` to `acct:b` fits it:

```text
MULTI
DECRBY acct:a 3000
INCRBY acct:b 3000
EXEC
```

No client can ever read `acct:a` debited and `acct:b` not yet credited. A batch has two limits. First, it can't decide. A GET inside MULTI also answers `QUEUED`, and its value arrives with all the other results at the end, too late to choose what to queue.

Second, it never rolls back. A command that Redis rejects while queuing, such as one with the wrong number of arguments, makes EXEC fail with `EXECABORT`, and nothing runs. But a command that fails while it runs, such as `INCR` (add one) on a key that holds a shop's name, fails alone, and the commands around it still run. In the words of the docs, "Redis does not support rollbacks of transactions". So if you know transactions from a database like PostgreSQL, read MULTI/EXEC as a batch that nothing can interrupt, not as all-or-nothing.

For a decision your code makes, Redis offers a check instead of a lock. `WATCH balance:7` notes that this connection depends on that key. You GET the balance, decide in your code that 100 is enough for 30, then send `MULTI`, `SET balance:7 70`, `EXEC`. If any client wrote `balance:7` after your WATCH, even the same value again, EXEC runs nothing and answers nil, Redis's word for no value, and you start over: watch, read, decide. This is check-and-set with a retry loop, and the stepper replays the lost update with it. Redis never makes anyone wait. It refuses a decision made from a stale read, one that has gone out of date since.

Three details matter in code. First, WATCH belongs to a connection, so WATCH, MULTI and EXEC must travel over the same one. Jedis, a Java library for Redis, has `redis.transaction(false)`. It holds one connection from the pool (the set of open connections a program shares) and runs commands at once until you call `multi()`. Lettuce, another Java library, shares one connection between callers, so a WATCH transaction needs a connection of its own. Second, watch only what your decision reads: the credit is an `INCRBY`, which is correct whatever the other account holds. Third, retries cost round trips, so on a key that many copies write, most attempts lose.

Redis 8 added one-command versions for a single key. `SET balance:7 70 IFEQ 100` (8.4) writes only if the value is still 100. `INCREX balance:7 BYINT -30 LBOUND 0` (8.8) subtracts 30 only if the result stays at 0 or above. Neither helps when the decision spans two keys. For that, there's a script, next.

stepper.title: WATCH turns a lost update into a retry
stepper.intro: The same two debits as the simulator, now with WATCH. Pod A and pod B are the two copies of the payments program.

frames.say: Both pods start the same way: `WATCH balance:7`, then `GET balance:7`, which returns 100. Redis records, for each connection, which keys it watches. Each pod decides in its own code that 100 is enough: pod A plans to write 70, and pod B plans to write 50.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 290" role="img" aria-label="Pod B's transaction runs and marks pod A's watch dirty"><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="180" height="196" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-m" x="110" y="42" text-anchor="middle">pod A (coffee, 30)</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="34" y="70" text-anchor="start">WATCH balance:7</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="34" y="94" text-anchor="start">GET balance:7 > 100</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="34" y="118" text-anchor="start">(computing 70)</text><rect class="box-ok" x="440" y="20" width="180" height="196" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-m" x="530" y="42" text-anchor="middle">pod B (fuel, 50)</text><text class="t-s t-code t-a" x="454" y="70" text-anchor="start">MULTI</text><text class="t-s t-code t-a" x="454" y="94" text-anchor="start">SET balance:7 50</text><text class="t-s t-code t-ok" x="454" y="118" text-anchor="start">EXEC > 1) OK</text><rect class="box-a" x="230" y="20" width="180" height="196" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-m" x="320" y="42" text-anchor="middle">Redis</text><text class="t t-code t-a" x="320" y="72" text-anchor="middle">balance:7 = 50</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="320" y="98" text-anchor="middle">watched by A</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="320" y="124" text-anchor="middle">A: dirty</text><text class="t-s t-ok" x="320" y="150" text-anchor="middle">B: done</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="232" width="600" height="46" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="320" y="260" text-anchor="middle">B's EXEC writes balance:7, and Redis marks every other connection watching it as dirty.</text></svg>
frames.say: Pod B is faster: `MULTI`, `SET balance:7 50` (which answers `QUEUED`), `EXEC`. Its watch is clean, so EXEC runs the SET, and the balance is 50. Any write to a watched key, even one that writes the same value again, marks every connection watching that key as **dirty**. Pod A's watch is now dirty, and pod A doesn't know yet.

B's debit survives.</text></svg>
frames.say: Pod A sends `MULTI`, `SET balance:7 70`, `EXEC`. Without WATCH, this is where 50 became 70 and B's debit was lost. Now EXEC checks the flag first, finds it dirty, throws the queued SET away and answers `(nil)`. EXEC also clears the connection's watches, whatever the outcome.

Both debits are in the balance.</text></svg>
frames.say: Nil means "you lost the race, start over". Pod A watches again, reads 50, checks that 30 still fits, and writes 20 in a new transaction. Nobody touched the key this time, so EXEC runs. The balance is 20, and both debits counted. This loop is the lab's `WatchTransfer`.

On a hot key, attempts keep failing.</text></svg>
frames.say: WATCH is optimistic: it assumes clashes are rare and pays only when one happens. On a key that 50 pods write all the time, most attempts lose, and each lost attempt costs several round trips. When one key is that busy, send the decision to Redis as a script instead, which never needs to retry.

try.title: Watch a batch keep going, then make EXEC refuse
steps: Open two redis-cli prompts: `docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli` in two terminals, from the `labs` folder.
Terminal 1: run the first block, two batches. Before each `EXEC`, predict the results. The `INCR` targets a key that holds `hello`, and the second batch has an `INCRBY` with no amount.

Terminal 1: run the WATCH block up to the `GET`. Then, in terminal 2, spend most of the money behind its back: `DECRBY balance:7 8000`. Back in terminal 1, run the rest, and predict what `EXEC` answers.

code.title: terminal 1 (lines starting with # are notes)
code.src:
# two batches
SET acct:a 10000
SET acct:b 0
SET acct:note hello
MULTI
DECRBY acct:a 3000
INCR acct:note
INCRBY acct:b 3000
EXEC
MULTI
DECRBY acct:a 3000
INCRBY acct:b
EXEC
MGET acct:a acct:b
# check-and-set
SET balance:7 10000
WATCH balance:7
GET balance:7
# now switch to terminal 2 and run: DECRBY balance:7 8000
MULTI
DECRBY balance:7 3000
EXEC
GET balance:7
# Redis 8.4 and 8.8: one-command check-and-set
SET balance:7 7000 IFEQ 10000
SET balance:7 1000 IFEQ 2000
INCREX balance:7 BYINT -3000 LBOUND 0
GET balance:7

try.expect:
In the batches, each queued command answers `QUEUED`. The first `EXEC` prints `1) (integer) 7000`, `2) (error) ERR value is not an integer or out of range` and `3) (integer) 3000`. The INCR failed alone, and the transfer around it still happened, so `MGET` shows `"7000"` and `"3000"`. In the second batch, the bad `INCRBY` is rejected at once with `(error) ERR wrong number of arguments for 'incrby' command`, and `EXEC` answers `(error) EXECABORT Transaction discarded because of previous errors.` Nothing ran: `MGET` still shows 7000 and 3000.

Terminal 1's `GET` prints `"10000"`, and terminal 2's `DECRBY` prints `(integer) 2000`. Terminal 1's `EXEC` prints `(nil)`: the watched key changed, so the queued DECRBY never ran, and `GET` shows `"2000"`, not -1000. `SET balance:7 7000 IFEQ 10000` prints `(nil)` because the value is 2000, and `SET balance:7 1000 IFEQ 2000` prints `OK`. `INCREX balance:7 BYINT -3000 LBOUND 0` answers `1) (integer) 1000` and `2) (integer) 0`: the debit would go below 0, so it applied nothing, and the balance stays `"1000"`.

refs.title: Transactions: errors and why there is no rollback

sections.h: A Lua script is a stored procedure: the whole decision runs on the thread
sections.body:
WATCH tells you that you lost a race. A script removes the race. It's the stored procedure of the first section: you send the logic to Redis, and Redis runs all of it on its one thread as one command.

`EVAL` takes the Lua source, the number of key names that follow, the keys, and then any other arguments. Inside the script they're `KEYS[1]`, `KEYS[2]` and `ARGV[1]`, and `redis.call` runs a Redis command and returns its result:

```text
EVAL "local b = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
      if b < tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end
      redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
      redis.call('INCRBY', KEYS[2], ARGV[1])
      return 1" 2 acct:a acct:b 3000
```

The script reads the balance of `acct:a` and returns 0 if it's less than the amount. Otherwise it moves the amount to `acct:b` and returns 1. This lesson's model says what happens next: the script runs from its first line to its last, and no other command runs in between. The read, the test and both writes happen together, with one round trip and no retries. Pass every key the script touches in KEYS, and don't build key names inside the script. Redis Cluster sends the call to a machine by its KEYS, as the last section shows.

The price is the other half of the model: one slow transaction stalls every client. Keep scripts short, with an end you can see: a transfer, or a check-and-update of one counter, never a loop over a big key. And a script doesn't roll back either. If it fails halfway, the writes before the failure stay, so check everything first and write last.

Sending the whole source on every call wastes network traffic, so Redis keeps a script cache. `SCRIPT LOAD` returns the script's SHA1 digest, a 40-character fingerprint of its text, and `EVALSHA <sha> ...` runs the cached script. The cache doesn't last. A restart, a failover (a replica, a copy of Redis on another machine, taking over) or `SCRIPT FLUSH` empties it, and EVALSHA then fails with `NOSCRIPT`. Every client must catch that, load the script again and retry. Jedis throws `JedisNoScriptException`, and the lab handles it.

Redis 7.0 added **functions** for logic that should live with the data. `FUNCTION LOAD` installs a named library of Lua functions, and `FCALL transfer 2 acct:a acct:b 1000` calls one. Redis saves libraries with the data and copies them to replicas, so they survive restarts and failovers. Use functions for logic that several programs share, and EVAL or EVALSHA for logic that ships with one program.

VoltDB asks one more thing of its procedures. It keeps its replicas in step by running the same procedure on each one, so a procedure must be deterministic: the same input must produce the same writes everywhere. Even the current time must come from VoltDB, not from the machine's clock. Redis could copy scripts to replicas that way until 7.0. Now it always sends replicas the writes a script made instead.

A script is the right tool whenever you can send the whole decision at once. Next, we'll meet the two limits that are left.

try.title: Load, lose and reload a script
steps: At a redis-cli prompt, set two balances and load the transfer script. `SCRIPT LOAD` prints its SHA1 digest. The commands below already use it, because the same script text always gives the same digest.
Run the two `EVALSHA`s. Predict both answers: the second asks for 9,000 when 7,000 is left.
Run `SCRIPT FLUSH` (what a restart or failover does to the cache) and the same `EVALSHA` again. Then install the same logic as a function, and call it with `FCALL`.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.src:
SET acct:a 10000
SET acct:b 0
SCRIPT LOAD "local b = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0') if b < tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) redis.call('INCRBY', KEYS[2], ARGV[1]) return 1"
EVALSHA 3ccbfe4f9ff6e5e06c85208eb88919f00da7b626 2 acct:a acct:b 3000
EVALSHA 3ccbfe4f9ff6e5e06c85208eb88919f00da7b626 2 acct:a acct:b 9000
SCRIPT FLUSH
EVALSHA 3ccbfe4f9ff6e5e06c85208eb88919f00da7b626 2 acct:a acct:b 3000
FUNCTION LOAD "#!lua name=ledger\nredis.register_function('transfer', function(keys, args) local b = tonumber(redis.call('GET', keys[1]) or '0') if b < tonumber(args[1]) then return 0 end redis.call('DECRBY', keys[1], args[1]) redis.call('INCRBY', keys[2], args[1]) return 1 end)"
FCALL transfer 2 acct:a acct:b 1000
MGET acct:a acct:b
FUNCTION DELETE ledger

try.expect: `SCRIPT LOAD` prints `"3ccbfe4f9ff6e5e06c85208eb88919f00da7b626"`. The first `EVALSHA` returns `(integer) 1` (moved), and the second `(integer) 0` (not enough money, nothing written). After `SCRIPT FLUSH`, the same `EVALSHA` fails with `(error) NOSCRIPT No matching script. Please use EVAL.` `FUNCTION LOAD` prints the library name, `"ledger"`, `FCALL` returns `(integer) 1`, and `MGET` shows `"6000"` and `"4000"`. `FUNCTION DELETE` prints `OK`. A function would still be there after a restart, and a cached script would not.

sections.h: The two limits: waiting for replies, and one thread per partition
sections.body:
A serial engine has two limits, and the first section's Try it showed the first. One client that waits for each reply got about 26,000 SETs a second from a thread that can run almost 1.9 million. The thread sat idle while each reply crossed the network and the next request came back. Many clients at once fill the gaps, and so does **pipelining**: sending many commands without waiting for each reply, then reading all the replies.

From a Java program on the laptop, through Docker's network, 5,000 SETs one at a time took 1.1 to 1.6 seconds, and one Jedis pipeline took about 10 ms. Lettuce pipelines without being asked. Its calls return at once, so 5,000 calls are all on their way before the first reply arrives, though by default it still sends each command as you make it.

A pipeline is not a transaction. Redis reads pipelined commands off the connection in chunks of up to 16 KB, and it serves other clients between chunks. So another client's read can land between a pipelined DECRBY and INCRBY. One command's reply also can't shape the next command in the same pipeline. Use pipelines for bulk work whose commands you know in advance. Keep batches to around 10,000 commands, because Redis holds all the replies in memory until it can send them. The figure shows the difference.

The second limit is one processor core, the part of a processor that runs one thread at a time. To go past it, split the data into partitions and give each its own thread. H-Store ran one single-threaded partition per core, and VoltDB does the same. A transaction that touches one partition runs alone on that partition's thread, so throughput, the work done per second, grows with cores and machines.

A transaction that touches two partitions must run on both threads in lockstep, each waiting for the other. VoltDB reports about 1,000 cross-partition writes a second, far below its single-partition rate, and more machines don't raise it. So the way you split the data decides the speed. A transfer between two wallets of one customer is fast if both live in one partition, and slow if they don't.

Redis Cluster, which spreads one Redis over several machines, takes the strict line: it has no cross-partition transactions at all. It sorts keys into 16,384 slots by a hash, a number worked out from the key's name. MULTI/EXEC, commands on several keys and scripts work only when every key lands in the same slot, and otherwise fail with `CROSSSLOT`. Hash tags put related keys together: in `{wallet:7}:main` and `{wallet:7}:hold`, only the part in braces is hashed. Partitioning: consistent hashing and hot keys covered how keys map to partitions, and Redis Cluster and production operations, in the Caching track, covers the slots.

**Serial execution is fast while each transaction stays on one thread. Keep what changes together in one partition.** The next lesson takes on the case serial engines avoid: committing one transaction on several machines.

try.title: Time 5,000 SETs three ways
steps: From the `labs` folder, run `PipelineDemo` (Java, with Jedis and Lettuce futures) or `PipelineDemoKt` (Kotlin, with Jedis and Lettuce coroutines). A future and a coroutine are both ways to start a call now and collect its answer later.
Predict the ratio between the first two lines before you look.
Run it twice. Which line moves most between runs, and what does that tell you about where the time goes?

code.title: PipelineDemo.java

alt.title: PipelineDemo.kt

try.expect: Four runs on the lab laptop: one by one took 1,101 to 1,642 ms (3,000 to 4,500 SETs a second), one Jedis pipeline 8 to 11 ms (440,000 to 610,000 SETs a second), Lettuce async 147 to 159 ms and Lettuce coroutines 200 to 224 ms. The one-by-one line moves most, because it's almost all round trips through Docker's network, and those vary. The pipeline is 100 to 180 times faster, with the same commands on the same server.

refs.title: Redis Cluster specification (hash slots, hash tags, multi-key operations)

mistake: The most common mistake is to read MULTI/EXEC as a database transaction. Code queues a debit and a credit, an error at run time hits one of them, and the developer expects nothing to have changed. Redis ran everything else, so the money moved halfway. The second mistake is to treat a pipeline as all-or-nothing because its commands left the client together, while other clients' commands run between them on the server. Both come from carrying a database's meaning of "transaction" over to Redis. Check inputs before EXEC, use a Lua script when a decision depends on what you read, and use pipelines only for speed.

compare.title: A MULTI/EXEC transfer in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Transfer.java

kotlin.title: Transfer.kt
kotlin.src:
// a transfer as one MULTI/EXEC batch; each queued command returns a Response
redis.multi().use { tx ->
    val from: Response<Long> = tx.decrBy("acct:a", 3_000)
    val to: Response<Long> = tx.incrBy("acct:b", 3_000)
    val results: List<Any>? = tx.exec()              // both run here, nothing in between
    println("${from.get()} ${to.get()}")             // 7000 3000
}

compare.note: The commands on the wire are the same in both: MULTI, DECRBY, INCRBY, EXEC. Inside the block, each call returns a `Response` that stays empty until `exec()`, and calling `get()` on it earlier throws, because Redis has only answered `QUEUED`. `exec()` returns null when a WATCH stopped the transaction, so Kotlin types it `List<Any>?` and makes you check. Java's try-with-resources and Kotlin's `use` both close the transaction object, which hands its connection back to the pool. Notice what neither version can do: look at the balance before deciding to debit. That needs WATCH or a script.

worked.title: Debit a prepaid card without going below zero

steps.say: The starting point loses updates: two copies of the program can both read 100 and both write. Inside an in-memory store: how Redis executes commands showed the same pattern losing four increments in five.
steps.alt_code:
val balance = redis.get(key)!!.toLong()
if (balance < amount) return false
redis.set(key, (balance - amount).toString())       // another pod may have written since the GET
return true

steps.say: Move the decision onto the server. The script reads, tests and writes inside one command, so nothing can run in between, and there's nothing to retry.
steps.code:
static final String DEBIT = """
        local b = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
        if b < tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end
        redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
        return 1
        """;
boolean ok = Long.valueOf(1).equals(redis.eval(DEBIT, List.of(key), List.of(String.valueOf(amount))));
steps.alt_code:
val DEBIT = """
    local b = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
    if b < tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end
    redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
    return 1
""".trimIndent()
val ok = redis.eval(DEBIT, listOf(key), listOf(amount.toString())) == 1L

steps.say: On Redis 8.8, the single-key case is one built-in command. `INCREX ... BYINT -amount LBOUND 0` answers with the new value and the amount it applied, and 0 applied means the debit was refused.
steps.code:
List<Long> reply = redis.increx(key, -amount, IncrexParams.increxParams().lbound(0));
boolean ok = reply.get(1) != 0;                      // [new balance, applied amount]
steps.alt_code:
val (newBalance, applied) = redis.increx(key, -amount, IncrexParams.increxParams().lbound(0))
val ok = applied != 0L                               // [new balance, applied amount]

steps.say: Pick by the shape of the decision. One key and Redis 8.8: INCREX. Several keys, or Redis before 8.8 (or Valkey, a free project that split off from Redis in 2024): a script, sent with EVALSHA and reloaded on NOSCRIPT. Logic that must stay in your program and rarely clashes: WATCH with a retry loop. The lab builds the two general ones for a two-key transfer.

lab.title: A transfer with WATCH, the same transfer in Lua, and a pipelined bulk load
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All 11 fail: five in `WatchTransferTest` and six in `ScriptedLedgerTest`, all against one shared Redis container. Balances are whole cents, stored as plain strings.

In `WatchTransfer.java`, write `transfer` as the javadoc describes: a loop of attempts, each with `redis.transaction(false)`, `watch`, a read, `multi`, two queued commands and `exec`. Run `./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.txn.l06.WatchTransferTest'`.

Read the test `a change to the watched balance aborts EXEC ...`. Its hook spends 8,000 cents from another client between your read and your EXEC, exactly once. Your transfer must notice on attempt 1 and refuse on attempt 2.
In `ScriptedLedger.kt`, replace the `TRANSFER` placeholder with the Lua script. Then write `transfer` with `evalsha` and a NOSCRIPT fallback, and `openAccounts` with one pipeline.
Run all 11 tests. Both 50-thread tests check that 2,000 random transfers neither create nor destroy a cent, and never overdraw.
hints: `tx.get(from).get()` before `tx.multi()` returns the value at once. Treat a missing balance as 0.
After `tx.multi()`, `tx.decrBy` and `tx.incrBy` only queue. `tx.exec()` returns null when the watched key changed, so go round the loop again.

In Lua: `local balance = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')`, compare it with `tonumber(ARGV[1])`, then two `redis.call`s and `return 1`. Script numbers come back to Jedis as `Long`, so compare the result with `1L`.
`redis.evalsha(sha, listOf(from, to), listOf(amount.toString()))`. Catch `redis.clients.jedis.exceptions.JedisNoScriptException`, call `redis.scriptLoad(TRANSFER)` again, and retry once.

drill.title: The WATCH retry loop from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write `transfer(from, to, amount)` with Jedis's `RedisClient`: WATCH the source, read it, refuse an overdraft, queue DECRBY and INCRBY in MULTI, and retry when EXEC returns null. Then compare. Which key did you watch, and why not both?

recap: Serial execution: one thread runs each transaction to the end before the next, so the result is always some one-at-a-time order, with no locks, deadlocks or clash aborts. It became practical once data fit in memory and everyday transactions proved tiny: H-Store ran 70,416 TPC-C transactions a second against 850 for a commercial database.

The thread must never wait for the client, so each transaction has to arrive complete, as a stored procedure. Redis runs each command, batch and script alone, and a GET then a SET from your program are two transactions that can lose an update.
MULTI/EXEC runs a queued batch with nothing in between. It can't branch on a read, and it never rolls back: a command that fails at run time fails alone.

WATCH makes EXEC refuse if a watched key was written since, which turns read-then-write into check-and-set with a retry. Redis 8.4's `SET ... IFEQ` and 8.8's `INCREX ... LBOUND` do it for one key in one command.

A Lua script is Redis's stored procedure: the read, the test and the writes in one command. Cache it with SCRIPT LOAD, call it with EVALSHA and reload it on NOSCRIPT. Functions (7.0) are saved with the data.

The limits: one core (pipelining saves round trips but isn't a transaction), and work across partitions. VoltDB runs that in lockstep at about 1,000 writes a second, and Redis Cluster refuses it with CROSSSLOT.

quiz.q: Program A runs `WATCH balance:7`, then `GET balance:7`, which returns 100. Before A's EXEC, another client runs `SET balance:7 100`, writing the same value again. A then sends `MULTI`, `SET balance:7 70`, `EXEC`. What does A get?
options: `(nil)`: any write to a watched key stops EXEC, even of the same value
`1) OK`: the value didn't change, so the watch still holds
An error: two clients can't watch the same key
`1) OK`, but only if both clients use the same connection pool
quiz.why: WATCH doesn't compare values. Every write command to the key marks every connection watching it as dirty, and EXEC on a dirty connection runs nothing. A plain GET by another client wouldn't have stopped it. If you want to compare values instead, Redis 8.4's `SET ... IFEQ` does exactly that.

quiz.q: A serial engine needs 10 µs of work per transfer. Version A drives each transfer one step at a time (read, decide in its own code, write and commit): two round trips of 0.5 ms, and the engine keeps its thread for the transfer until it commits. Version B sends the same logic as a stored procedure. Roughly how many transfers a second can each reach?
options: A: about 100,000; B: about 100,000, because the work is the same
A: about 50,000; B: about 100,000
A: unlimited, because there are no locks; B: about 100,000
A: about 1,000; B: about 100,000, because B's thread never waits for the client
quiz.why: In A, the only thread waits 1 ms per transfer for 10 µs of work, so it manages about 1,000 a second. In B, the round trips overlap with other clients' procedures, and the thread only does the work: 1 second divided by 10 µs is 100,000. Counting only the processor's work is the tempting mistake. This is why serial engines require stored procedures, and why Redis serves other clients between your commands instead of waiting for you.

quiz.q: A Lua transfer script runs as one command. Why is a script that loops over a set of 2 million members to work out a balance a bad idea?
options: Lua scripts can't read sets
It runs on the one thread that runs every command, so every client waits until it finishes
Redis kills any script after 5 seconds
Scripts run on a background thread and see old data
quiz.why: Running alone and blocking everyone are the same fact: nothing else runs while the script runs. A loop over 2 million members takes long enough that every client, whatever key it wants, waits behind it. After 5 seconds (`busy-reply-threshold`), other clients start getting BUSY errors, but Redis doesn't kill the script. You'd have to send SCRIPT KILL.

quiz.q: 50 pods (running copies of the payments program) take money from the same busy wallet key about 2,000 times a second, with a WATCH/MULTI/EXEC retry loop. The slowest payments keep getting slower. What's the best change?
options: Raise the connection pool size, so more attempts run in parallel
Add a random pause before each retry, and keep WATCH
Move the read, test and write into a Lua script (or INCREX on Redis 8.8), so there's nothing to retry
Wrap each attempt in a pipeline
quiz.why: WATCH is optimistic. On a busy key most attempts lose, each lost attempt costs several round trips, and more attempts in parallel only make more of them lose. A script runs the whole decision as one command, so it never clashes and never retries. A pipeline doesn't change the clash, and a pause only trades retries for waiting.

quiz.q: From Concurrency control: why does Redis need no deadlock detector, even for batches and scripts that touch several keys?
options: Nothing ever waits for a lock: the one thread runs each command, batch or script to the end before starting the next, so no cycle of waits can form
It has one, and it runs after a timeout, as PostgreSQL's does
Deadlocks can happen, but a failover breaks them
Its keys are too small to need locks
quiz.why: A deadlock is a cycle of transactions, each waiting for a lock another holds, and that lesson's detector searches the waits-for graph for one. In a serial engine, no transaction waits while holding anything, so there's no graph to search. The cost moved somewhere else: a slow script makes every client wait, the opposite trade from locks on single rows.

flashcards.front: What does EXEC do when one queued command fails at run time?
flashcards.back: It runs all the others and returns an error in that command's place. Redis never rolls back.

flashcards.front: When does a whole Redis transaction fail with EXECABORT?
flashcards.back: When a command was rejected while queuing (bad syntax, wrong number of arguments). Then nothing runs.

flashcards.front: What makes a WATCHed EXEC return nil?
flashcards.back: Any write to a watched key by any client after the WATCH, even of the same value. The client should read again and retry.

flashcards.front: Why did serial execution become practical?
flashcards.back: Memory got cheap enough to hold the data in use, so transactions don't wait for the disk, and everyday transactions are tiny: TPC-C's heaviest reads about 200 records.

flashcards.front: Why must a serial engine get the whole transaction at once?
flashcards.back: Otherwise its one thread waits for the client's round trips: 1 ms of waiting per 10 µs of work caps it near 1,000 transactions a second. So it runs stored procedures.
No. It saves round trips, but other clients' commands can run between pipelined commands.

flashcards.front: What does a cross-partition transaction cost a serial engine?
flashcards.back: Every partition it touches must run it in lockstep. VoltDB reports about 1,000 cross-partition writes a second, far below its single-partition rate, and Redis Cluster refuses them with CROSSSLOT.

terms.plain: Running transactions one at a time on one thread, so no locks or conflict checks are needed.
A whole transaction sent to the database as code that it runs to the end: Java classes in VoltDB, Lua scripts in Redis.
Two clients read the same value and both write, and the second write silently replaces the first.
Queue commands after MULTI, then run them all at EXEC with nothing in between. There's no rollback.
Makes the next EXEC on this connection run nothing if any watched key was written in the meantime.
A Lua function installed with FUNCTION LOAD and called with FCALL. It's saved and copied to replicas with the data.
Sending many commands without waiting for each reply, then reading all the replies.

explain_back.prompt: A friend wants to protect a wallet debit (check the balance, then subtract) by sending the GET and the SET in one pipeline, "so they run together". Explain why that doesn't work and what you'd use instead.
explain_back.answer: A pipeline only stops the client from waiting for each reply before it sends the next command. Redis still runs the commands one by one, and it serves other clients between them, so another program's write can land between our GET and our SET. Worse, in a pipeline we don't even have the GET's answer before the SET is sent, so the SET can't depend on it. Wrapping them in MULTI/EXEC doesn't help either, because queued commands can't use each other's results. The decision needs the read, the check and the write to happen with nothing in between. I'd use a short Lua script that reads the balance, refuses if it's too low, and subtracts, called with EVALSHA and reloaded on NOSCRIPT. On Redis 8.8, a single-key debit with a floor is one command, `INCREX key BYINT -amount LBOUND 0`. WATCH with a retry loop also works, but on a busy wallet it retries a lot.

deeper.body:
**Scripts can say what they do.** A script can start with a line like `#!lua flags=no-writes`, and Redis then knows it only reads. It may run on a replica, and it's allowed while the server is out of memory. Without flags, a script is treated as one that may write. Functions take the same flags through `redis.register_function{function_name=..., callback=..., flags={'no-writes'}}`, and `FCALL_RO` runs a read-only function on a replica.

**Time stands still inside a script.** Since Redis 7.0, Redis takes the time once when a script starts, and every command inside it sees that moment: `TIME` returns the same value, and key expiry is judged against it. The ExpiryDemo in Expiry, eviction and memory, in the Caching track, relies on this: 500,000 `SET ... PX 3000` calls in one script all got the same deadline. It's also why a busy loop that waits on `TIME` never ends.

**How scripts reach replicas.** Redis 7.0 changed this too. Redis no longer sends the script itself to replicas. It sends the write commands the script produced, which is called effects replication. That's why a script may now use random numbers and the current time freely: replicas never run it again, so they can't work out something different.

**Memory limits.** Transactions and scripts are both checked against `maxmemory`, the memory limit set for the server, before they start (Expiry, eviction and memory covers it). Once a script has written something, Redis lets it finish even if memory runs out, because stopping halfway would break its promise to run as one step. The same rule makes a long script dangerous in a second way: SCRIPT KILL only works on a script that hasn't written yet.

**Deterministic databases.** These push serial execution further. Calvin (Thomson and colleagues, 2012) first agrees, across all partitions, on the order of the transactions' inputs. Then every partition runs them in that order, the same way each time, so no partition ever has to ask another whether to commit. The price is that a transaction must say up front which keys it will read and write: no interactive transactions, as in this lesson. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 8, puts serial execution, two-phase locking and SSI side by side.

sources.title: Stonebraker et al.: The End of an Architectural Era (It's Time for a Complete Rewrite), VLDB 2007

opening:
Picture a small café with one barista. She makes one drink at a time and never starts the next until it's handed over. Nobody fights over the milk jug, because there's only one pair of hands. With short orders, the queue still moves fast.

Redis, a program that keeps data in memory and answers short commands, works the same way. One thread, a single line of work, runs every command in turn. So it's tempting to think anything you send it is safe, since nothing runs at once. Then a prepaid card with 100.00 on it pays for a 30.00 coffee and 50.00 of fuel at once, and ends up with 50.00 left instead of 20.00.

In Concurrency control, the PostgreSQL database let transactions run at the same time and sorted out the clashes with locks and checks. In this lesson, we'll try the opposite, one thread and no locks, and see why it's fast, why the card still lost money, and which Redis tool fixes it. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a prepaid card that paid 80.00 and lost only 50.00, on a server that runs one command at a time. The thread was never the problem. Two commands are two transactions, and the fix is to send the whole decision at once as a script, or to check it with WATCH.

With Redis running, start `redis-cli MONITOR` in one terminal to print every command the server runs, and do this lesson's Try its in another. Look for a GET followed later by a SET on the same key. That's a decision made across two transactions.

Next, we'll leave the single machine and commit one transaction on two. What happens when one says yes and the other never answers?
